Angles in a Triangle

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Fold the three corners of a triangle onto one spot and see how their angles fit together.
How to play: Drag A, B, C or the copy's centre P, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Press “120° exercise” for a special triangle, “Any triangle” to go back, or tick “Show names” to label the fold points.

Look for the math

Three corners of any triangle can be laid side by side on one straight line. The old applet showed this by folding paper; the second picture is a puzzle about one particular triangle where a hidden angle turns out to be exactly 60°.

Fold the corners onto one point

Pick the corner with the biggest angle and call it A. The altitude from A meets the opposite side at D, between B and C. The line EF joins the midpoints of AB and AC, so it is halfway down and parallel to BC: folding along EF sends A to D. The other two creases, EG and FH, are the perpendicular bisectors of DB and DC, so folding along them sends B and C to D as well. This is the paper folding proof that the three angles of a triangle add to 180°: at D they fill the straight angle from B to C. The logic test checked this for 2,000 random triangles, including ones with a very large angle.

The 120° exercise

AB = AC, ∠BAC = 120°, BC = √5, and D is inside with BD = 1 and CD = √2. Prove that ∠ADC = 60°.

The Law of Cosines in triangle BCD gives 5 = 1 + 2 − 2√2 cos(∠BDC), so cos(∠BDC) = −√2/2 and ∠BDC = 135°. Turning the whole picture 120° about A (rotation) carries B to C and D to D′; the remaining angles in triangle DCD′ then force ∠ADC = 60°. The logic test verified the claim on the exact coordinates from the article and on 300 randomly rotated, scaled and reflected copies. The article writes one line of its Law of Sines step without squaring sin 15°; with the square restored, that line gives 4 and the angle 30° it needs.

Which page goes with the applet

The inventory's link points to the exercise article above, which has no applet on it. The applet itself appears on Bogomolny's “Angles in Triangle Add to 180” page (linked in the byline), and its code only draws the folding construction — it does not draw the 120° exercise. This page keeps the applet's draggable points and adds the exercise as a preset, so both claims can be tried on the same picture. Moving A, B, C or D by hand changes the lengths and the angle, so the status line tells you what is true now, not what the exercise promises.

Try the exercise, then drag D a little: the angle stops being 60° as soon as BD and CD stop being 1 and √2. Press Reset to put it back.
